cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk despite elevated mood. Risk from impulsivity, risk-taking behavior, and 'crash' into depression. Mixed features increase risk
cases.explanation: Bipolar I Disorder requires at least one lifetime manic episode. Mania is defined as elevated/irritable mood plus 3+ additional symptoms (4 if mood is only irritable) for ≥1 week or requiring hospitalization. This patient has severe mania with 7 B-symptoms: decreased sleep, talkativeness/pressured speech, flight of ideas, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity, excessive pleasurable activities with high risk. Cocaine use complicates but history of previous depression and family history support primary bipolar disorder. Lithium non-adherence is common trigger for relapse
cases.management: ACUTE MANAGEMENT (Psychiatric Emergency): (1) Urgent psychiatric assessment - likely requires involuntary admission given poor insight and risk; (2) Safe environment, low stimulation; (3) Pharmacological: Resume mood stabilizer (lithium 600-900mg, aim therapeutic 0.6-1.2) PLUS antipsychotic for rapid control (olanzapine 15-20mg or risperidone 2-4mg); (4) Benzodiazepines PRN for agitation (lorazepam 1-2mg); (5) Monitor for metabolic decompensation, dehydration; (6) Substance use counseling; (7) Restrict access to finances, car keys. ONGOING: (8) Psychoeducation about bipolar disorder; (9) Address medication adherence - why stopped lithium? Side effects? (10) Regular lithium monitoring; (11) Family psychoeducation; (12) Relapse prevention planning; (13) Vocational rehabilitation post-recovery; (14) Long-term mood stabilization

cases.mse: Appearance: Colorful clothing, bright makeup. Behavior: Animated, socially disinhibited. Speech: Increased rate and volume, some tangentiality. Mood: 'Great! So much energy!'. Affect: Elevated, expansive. Thought: Flight of ideas, some grandiosity (believes her artwork will definitely get into prestigious gallery). Perception: No abnormalities. Cognition: Distractible. cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate risk currently, but mixed states and post-manic depression are high-risk periods. History of previous depression increases concern
cases.explanation: This represents a manic episode of moderate severity - distinct period of elevated mood with ≥3 additional symptoms causing marked functional change but not severe enough to require hospitalization or with psychotic features. Critical diagnostic point: previous depression plus current mania = Bipolar I (not unipolar depression). Antidepressant (sertraline) may have precipitated switch to mania, which is common (10-25% risk). This changes diagnosis and long-term treatment approach fundamentally
cases.management: (1) Stop antidepressant immediately (sertraline likely precipitated mania); (2) Discuss diagnosis change to Bipolar I - implications for long-term treatment; (3) Initiate mood stabilizer: lithium (start 400mg BD, titrate), valproate (500-1000mg), or lamotrigine (slow titration); (4) Consider short-term antipsychotic if significant distress/impairment (low-dose quetiapine 200-400mg or olanzapine 10mg); (5) May manage as outpatient if good support and insight can be developed; (6) Monitor daily/every-other-day initially; (7) Sleep hygiene crucial - regularize sleep-wake cycle; (8) Reduce stimulation; (9) Psychoeducation about bipolar disorder, triggers, early warning signs; (10) Avoid future antidepressants without mood stabilizer; (11) Family involvement; (12) Long-term: maintenance mood stabilizer indefinitely after first manic episode

cases.duration: 5 days. History: Multiple depressive episodes over 10 years
cases.associated: Sleeping 4-5 hours only, feels more confident and creative, more talkative, started organizing long-postponed projects, increased work productivity, mild increased spending (not problematic), no impairment in functioning - actually functioning better than usual

cases.investigations: Blood: All normal. MDQ: Positive. YMRS: 14/60 (mild-moderate elevation).
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate long-term risk. Bipolar II has high lifetime suicide risk (similar to Bipolar I) despite less severe mania. Depressive episodes are more frequent and severe
cases.explanation: Bipolar II requires lifetime history of at least one hypomanic episode AND at least one major depressive episode. Hypomania differs from mania: (1) Duration ≥4 days (vs ≥7 for mania); (2) Noticeable change but WITHOUT marked impairment or hospitalization; (3) No psychotic features. Many patients with Bipolar II go years misdiagnosed as unipolar depression because hypomania feels good and patients don't report it. Clues include: multiple depressive episodes, atypical features, family history, antidepressant-induced mood elevation. Bipolar II is NOT a milder disorder - depressive burden is often greater
cases.management: (1) Diagnostic clarification - review lifetime mood episodes, educate about Bipolar II; (2) Mood stabilizer initiation: lamotrigine is preferred (targets depression more, less weight gain) - start 25mg, slow titration to 200mg over 6 weeks due to SJS risk; Alternative: lithium or valproate; (3) Current hypomania: may observe if mild and no risky behavior, or low-dose quetiapine 50-100mg; (4) If on antidepressant: controversial - some advocate discontinuing, others continuing with mood stabilizer cover; (5) Psychoeducation emphasizing depressive burden; (6) Mood monitoring - daily mood charts to identify patterns; (7) Lifestyle regularity - social rhythm therapy, consistent sleep-wake; (8) CBT adapted for bipolar disorder; (9) Identify early warning signs; (10) Long-term maintenance treatment essential; (11) Avoid triggers (stress management, avoid stimulants/alcohol)

cases.presenting_complaint: Long history of mood swings - ups and downs 'like a rollercoaster' for at least 3 years
cases.associated: Periods of high energy, creativity, sociability alternating with periods of low mood, low energy, pessimism. Neither extreme is severe enough to meet full criteria. Pattern is chaotic and unpredictable. Affects relationships and work consistency. Symptom-free periods never last more than 2 months
cases.risk_factors: Strong family history (father has Bipolar I, sister has Bipolar II), creative profession (musician), irregular lifestyle, substance use (cannabis)
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate. Behavior: Currently in 'normal' mood state. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Right now okay, but it changes constantly'. Affect: Euthymic currently. Thought: Describes pattern of mood reactivity to minor events. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Good - frustrated by mood instability
cases.investigations: Retrospective mood charting over 6 months shows multiple mood fluctuations without clear pattern. No single episode meets criteria for major depression or hypomania. No medical causes identified
cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate risk. Risk of progression to Bipolar I or II (15-50% over lifetime). Impulsivity during 'up' phases and despair during 'down' phases
cases.explanation: Cyclothymic Disorder is characterized by chronic fluctuating mood with numerous periods of hypomanic symptoms and depressive symptoms for ≥2 years (1 year in children/adolescents), without meeting full criteria for manic, hypomanic, or major depressive episodes. Symptom-free intervals last <2 months. Often begins in adolescence/early adulthood. Represents mild but chronic bipolar spectrum disorder. Strong predictor of developing full Bipolar I or II. Causes significant interpersonal and occupational difficulties due to unpredictability
cases.management: (1) Psychoeducation about cyclothymia and bipolar spectrum; (2) Mood stabilizer controversial but often recommended: lithium (may reduce progression to bipolar disorder), lamotrigine, or valproate; (3) Avoid antidepressants (may destabilize mood further); (4) Psychotherapy is CRUCIAL - interpersonal and social rhythm therapy (IPSRT) to regularize daily routines and sleep; (5) CBT to manage mood fluctuations and interpersonal consequences; (6) Daily mood monitoring; (7) Lifestyle interventions: regular sleep-wake schedule, avoid alcohol/drugs, exercise; (8) Address substance use; (9) Vocational counseling - may need career accommodations; (10) Long-term monitoring for progression to bipolar disorder; (11) Some patients choose to not take medication if functioning acceptable - respect autonomy while monitoring

cases.presenting_complaint: Feeling invincible, not sleeping, and engaging in risky behavior for 3 days following cocaine binge
cases.associated: Heavy cocaine use over weekend, now experiencing elevated mood, grandiosity, paranoia, decreased need for sleep, hypersexuality, irritability when cocaine unavailable, previous similar episodes always associated with cocaine use
cases.risk_factors: no personal or family history of primary mood disorder, started using cocaine 2 years ago at parties, now using weekly
cases.mse: Appearance: Disheveled, dilated pupils, nasal septum damage visible. Behavior: Agitated, hypervigilant, restless. Speech: Rapid, pressured. Mood: 'I feel amazing, but also they're watching me'. Affect: Labile - euphoric to irritable. Thought: Grandiose ideas, paranoid ideation (believes followed by police), flight of ideas. Perception: Possible visual illusions, no formed hallucinations currently. Cognition: Distractible. Insight: Poor
cases.investigations: Urine drug screen: Positive for cocaine, cannabis. Blood: Mild tachycardia on ECG. Timeline: Symptoms began during cocaine binge and persist due to continued use. No history of mood symptoms when abstinent
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate-high risk. Risk from impulsivity, paranoia, and severe 'crash' depression that follows cocaine binge (withdrawal phase). Also risk-taking behavior while intoxicated
cases.explanation: Substance-Induced Mood Disorder requires prominent mood symptoms that developed during or within 1 month of substance intoxication/withdrawal, and symptoms exceed those typically associated with intoxication/withdrawal. Cocaine (stimulant) directly causes dopamine surge leading to euphoria, grandiosity, decreased sleep, increased energy mimicking mania. Paranoia is also common with stimulants. Critical distinction from primary Bipolar Disorder: (1) Temporal relationship with substance use; (2) No mood episodes when abstinent; (3) Symptoms resolve with abstinence (though 'crash' depression follows stimulant withdrawal); (4) No family history of bipolar. Cocaine-induced mania typically lasts hours to days, not weeks
cases.management: ACUTE: (1) Supportive care in safe, low-stimulation environment; (2) Monitor vitals (tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia); (3) Benzodiazepines for agitation (lorazepam 1-2mg PRN); (4) Avoid antipsychotics initially (lower seizure threshold) unless severe psychosis; (5) Hydration; (6) ECG monitoring; (7) Address paranoia with reassurance and safety; (8) Observe for 'crash' phase (severe dysphoria, hypersomnia follows - may last days to weeks). ONGOING: (9) Motivational interviewing about cocaine use; (10) Addiction treatment referral; (11) Contingency management; (12) Treat comorbid disorders; (13) Address psychosocial factors; (14) Harm reduction if not ready for abstinence; (15) NO mood stabilizers or antipsychotics long-term if symptoms resolve with abstinence; (16) Follow-up to confirm diagnosis - if mood episodes recur without substance use, reconsider primary bipolar disorder

cases.presenting_complaint: Sudden onset of elevated mood, irritability, and insomnia 5 days after starting high-dose steroids for asthma exacerbation
cases.associated: Started prednisolone 60mg daily for acute asthma, developed rapid mood elevation, irritability, decreased sleep (2-3 hours), increased activity, talking excessively, shopping spree, anxiety, emotional lability
cases.risk_factors: No psychiatric history, no family history of mood disorder, previous courses of steroids without psychiatric effects (but lower doses)
cases.mse: Appearance: Appears activated. Behavior: Overactive, restless. Speech: Increased rate. Mood: 'Wired, can't settle'. Affect: Elevated but also anxious and irritable. Thought: Racing thoughts, mild grandiosity, preoccupied with multiple plans. Perception: No hallucinations. Cognition: Distractible. Insight: Partial - attributes to steroids
cases.investigations: Medical: Treated for acute asthma exacerbation with prednisolone 60mg daily started 5 days ago. Clear temporal relationship. No electrolyte abnormalities. YMRS: 18/60 (moderate symptoms)
cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate. Steroid-induced psychiatric symptoms increase risk. Monitor for mixed features or psychosis which can develop
cases.explanation: Corticosteroid-induced psychiatric symptoms occur in 5-18% of patients on moderate-to-high doses. Risk increases with dose (especially >40mg prednisone equivalent), rapidity of increase, and prior psychiatric history (though can occur in anyone). Presentations vary: mania/hypomania (most common), depression, mixed states, psychosis, anxiety, or delirium. Onset typically within first week but can occur anytime. Mechanism involves glucocorticoid effects on neurotransmitter systems and HPA axis. Symptoms resolve with dose reduction but may take days to weeks
cases.management: (1) Consult medical team urgently - can steroids be tapered or switched to different therapy? Dose reduction often resolves symptoms; (2) If steroids must continue: Start psychiatric medication - atypical antipsychotic (olanzapine 5-10mg or quetiapine 100-200mg preferred - evidence for steroid-induced symptoms) OR lithium or valproate (but drug interactions); (3) Avoid antidepressants (may worsen mania); (4) Benzodiazepines PRN for agitation/insomnia (lorazepam 0.5-1mg); (5) Monitor closely - symptoms can escalate to psychosis or severe mania; (6) Psychoeducation - reassure likely medication-related and reversible; (7) Safety planning; (8) Once steroids discontinued: taper psychiatric medications over 2-4 weeks if introduced; (9) Document in medical record - future steroid courses may require psychiatric prophylaxis; (10) Consider alternative to steroids if future need (e.g., steroid-sparing agents)

cases.presenting_complaint: Increasing irritability, restlessness, insomnia, and uncharacteristic impulsivity over 3 months
cases.associated: Can't sit still, palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss despite increased appetite, hand tremor, frequent bowel movements, irritability with family, started spending impulsively, racing thoughts, feeling 'sped up'
cases.risk_factors: No psychiatric history, family history of autoimmune thyroid disease, recent neck swelling noted by family
cases.mse: Appearance: Anxious, exophthalmos noted, visible tremor. Behavior: Restless, fidgety, overactive. Speech: Rapid rate. Mood: 'Irritable, can't relax'. Affect: Labile - irritable, anxious. Thought: Racing thoughts, mild pressure of speech, no clear grandiosity. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Distractible, complains of poor concentration. Insight: Attributes to being 'stressed'
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH <0.01, Free T4 42, Free T3 elevated. Positive TPO and TSH receptor antibodies. ECG: Sinus tachycardia 110bpm. Clinical signs: Fine tremor, warm moist skin, hyperreflexia, lid lag
cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate risk. Irritability and impulsivity from hyperthyroidism increase risk. Thyrotoxic crisis is medical emergency
cases.explanation: Hyperthyroidism (particularly Graves' disease) can cause psychiatric symptoms resembling mania: anxiety, irritability, insomnia, tremor, hyperactivity, emotional lability, and occasionally frank mania or psychosis ('thyrotoxic psychosis'). Mechanism involves thyroid hormone effects on adrenergic system and direct CNS effects. Key diagnostic features: (1) Medical symptoms (weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations); (2) Physical signs (tachycardia, tremor, goiter, eye signs if Graves'); (3) Abnormal thyroid function tests; (4) No previous psychiatric history. Important to distinguish from primary mania with coincidental hyperthyroidism
cases.management: PRIMARY TREATMENT IS MEDICAL: (1) Urgent endocrinology referral; (2) Initiate antithyroid medication (carbimazole 15-40mg daily OR propylthiouracil); (3) Beta-blocker for symptomatic relief (propranolol 40mg TDS) - addresses tremor, palpitations, anxiety AND psychiatric symptoms; (4) Monitor thyroid function every 4-6 weeks initially; (5) Symptoms should improve as thyroid levels normalize (may take 6-8 weeks); (6) If severe psychiatric symptoms: short-term antipsychotic (quetiapine 50-100mg) or benzodiazepine for agitation; (7) Avoid mood stabilizers unless symptoms persist after euthyroid state achieved; (8) Psychoeducation about medical cause of symptoms; (9) Monitor for emergence of hypothyroidism during treatment (can cause depression); (10) Definitive treatment options: radioiodine or thyroidectomy if medical management fails; (11) Reassess psychiatric symptoms once euthyroid for 2-3 months - if resolved, confirms secondary mania

cases.presenting_complaint: Simultaneous elevated and irritable mood with racing thoughts but also crying spells and hopelessness for 1 week
cases.associated: Elevated energy and decreased sleep (3 hours), racing thoughts, impulsive spending, hypersexuality, BUT ALSO dysphoria, crying episodes, feelings of hopelessness, death wishes, severe irritability and agitation. Extremely dysphoric and distressed despite elevated mood
cases.risk_factors: Bipolar I diagnosis 5 years ago, multiple previous pure manic and depressive episodes, stopped lithium 2 months ago, alcohol use
cases.mse: Appearance: Disheveled, agitated. Behavior: Psychomotor agitation, pacing. Speech: Pressured, loud. Mood: 'Everything at once - can't stand it, want to die'. Affect: Labile, dysphoric with anxious overlay. Thought: Racing thoughts, flight of ideas, BUT ALSO hopelessness, suicidal ideation ('can't live like this'). Perception: No hallucinations. Cognition: Distractible. Insight: Poor
cases.investigations: YMRS: 28/60. HAM-D: 18. Urine drug screen: Positive for alcohol. Clinical picture shows simultaneous manic AND depressive features
cases.suicide_risk: VERY HIGH RISK. Mixed episodes have highest suicide risk in bipolar disorder. Combination of depressive hopelessness, manic impulsivity, severe agitation, and disinhibition creates extremely dangerous situation. URGENT assessment required
cases.explanation: DSM-5 recognizes 'mixed features' specifier when predominant mood episode (manic or depressive) occurs with at least 3 symptoms of opposite pole. Previously called 'mixed episode' or 'dysphoric mania'. Characteristics: simultaneous elevated and depressed mood, severe irritability, psychomotor agitation, racing thoughts with negative content. Mixed states are associated with: HIGHEST suicide risk, more severe course, worse treatment response, more hospitalizations. Particularly dangerous because combines depressive hopelessness with manic impulsivity and energy. Often precipitated by antidepressants, substance use, or medication non-adherence
cases.management: PSYCHIATRIC EMERGENCY: (1) Urgent hospitalization - likely involuntary given high suicide risk; (2) One-to-one observation; (3) Remove means for self-harm; (4) AVOID ANTIDEPRESSANTS (can worsen mixed states). PHARMACOLOGICAL: (5) Mood stabilizer + antipsychotic combination is first-line: Valproate (loading dose possible: 20-30mg/kg, then 1000-2000mg/day) OR lithium (600-1200mg, rapid loading if safe) PLUS atypical antipsychotic (olanzapine 15-20mg, risperidone 2-4mg, OR quetiapine 300-600mg); (6) Benzodiazepines for severe agitation (lorazepam 2mg PRN); (7) Consider clozapine if refractory (evidence for mixed states); (8) ECT is highly effective for mixed states if medication fails or urgent response needed. (9) Alcohol detoxification if needed. ONGOING: (10) Intensive psychiatric monitoring; (11) Address medication non-adherence; (12) Psychoeducation about mixed states; (13) Long-term: maintenance medication crucial, often requires combination therapy; (14) Close outpatient follow-up post-discharge

cases.presenting_complaint: Elevated mood, claiming to have special powers, hearing God's voice telling him he is chosen, not sleeping for 4 days
cases.associated: Grandiose delusions (believes he is chosen by God for special mission), religious preoccupation, auditory hallucinations (God's voice), marked decreased sleep, extremely elevated mood, increased energy, impulsive behavior, hypersexuality, pressured speech
cases.risk_factors: Bipolar I disorder diagnosed 8 years ago, previous manic episodes without psychosis, recent stress (job loss), marijuana use, poor medication adherence
cases.mse: Appearance: Bizarre clothing choices, religious symbols. Behavior: Overactive, intrusive, disinhibited. Speech: Pressured, loud, tangential. Mood: 'Blessed! I am chosen!'. Affect: Euphoric, expansive. Thought: Grandiose delusions (special religious mission), delusional conviction, loose associations. Perception: Auditory hallucinations (God's voice commanding him, congruent with mood). Cognition: Unable to focus. Insight: Absent
cases.investigations: Urine drug screen: Positive for cannabis. Blood: No abnormalities. Previous records confirm bipolar diagnosis. CT head: Not indicated unless first episode or atypical features. YMRS: 42/60 (severe mania with psychosis)
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate-high risk. Psychotic mania has increased risk due to impulsivity, impaired judgment, and potential command hallucinations. Risk increases as mood shifts to depression
cases.explanation: Mania with psychotic features occurs in ~50-70% of manic episodes. Psychotic symptoms are typically mood-congruent (grandiose delusions, religious themes) but can be mood-incongruent. Presence of psychosis indicates severe episode requiring hospitalization. Differential diagnosis includes: (1) Bipolar I with psychotic features (most likely given history); (2) Schizoaffective disorder (requires psychosis outside mood episodes); (3) Substance-induced (cannabis can worsen but unlikely sole cause given bipolar history); (4) Primary psychotic disorder (schizophrenia - but prominent mood symptoms and previous bipolar episodes argue against). Cannabis use may have precipitated or exacerbated episode
cases.management: URGENT HOSPITALIZATION: (1) Involuntary admission likely needed; (2) Safe environment, low stimulation; (3) Frequent monitoring. PHARMACOLOGICAL: (4) Antipsychotic is ESSENTIAL (mood stabilizer alone insufficient for psychotic mania): High-potency: risperidone 2-4mg, haloperidol 5-15mg OR Broad-spectrum: olanzapine 15-20mg; (5) PLUS mood stabilizer: lithium or valproate (can combine initially if severe); (6) Benzodiazepines PRN (lorazepam 2mg); (7) IM medications if oral refused (haloperidol 5mg, olanzapine 10mg, lorazepam 2mg); (8) Monitor for neuroleptic malignant syndrome. ACUTE PHASE: (9) Reality orientation (gentle, non-confrontational); (10) Address cannabis use (motivational interviewing post-acute phase); (11) Liaise with family; (12) Once stable, gradually taper antipsychotic to lowest effective dose (some patients need maintenance). MAINTENANCE: (13) Optimize mood stabilizer; (14) May need long-acting injectable if adherence poor; (15) Substance abuse treatment; (16) Psychoeducation; (17) Relapse prevention; (18) Close outpatient follow-up

cases.presenting_complaint: Experiencing 6 distinct mood episodes (3 manic, 3 depressive) over the past 10 months
cases.duration: Pattern over 10 months (meets rapid cycling criterion of ≥4 episodes/year)
cases.associated: Clear episodes of mania (elevated mood, decreased sleep, impulsivity lasting 1-2 weeks) alternating with major depression (anhedonia, hypersomnia, suicidal ideation lasting 3-4 weeks). Brief euthymic periods between some episodes. Pattern has accelerated over past year
cases.risk_factors: Bipolar II for 8 years, initially stable on mood stabilizers, recent addition of antidepressant (may have induced cycling), hypothyroidism (poorly controlled TSH 8.2), female sex, substance use (alcohol)
cases.mse: Appearance: Currently in depressive phase - unkempt. Behavior: Psychomotor retardation. Speech: Slow. Mood: 'Exhausted from the rollercoaster, when will it end?'. Affect: Depressed. Thought: Hopelessness, demoralization about illness course. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Reduced concentration. Insight: Excellent - very aware of cycling pattern, frustrated
cases.investigations: Mood chart review: Documents 6 clear episodes in 10 months. TSH: 8.2 (hypothyroid - suboptimal control). Current medications: Lamotrigine 200mg, sertraline 100mg (added 1 year ago), levothyroxine 75mcg. Lithium level: Not on lithium currently
cases.suicide_risk: High risk. Rapid cycling associated with increased suicide risk, worse quality of life, treatment resistance. Patient expresses demoralization
cases.explanation: Rapid cycling is specifier in bipolar disorder defined as ≥4 mood episodes (manic, hypomanic, or depressive) in 12 months. Affects 10-20% of bipolar patients. Associated with: worse prognosis, increased suicide risk, more hospitalizations, treatment resistance. Risk factors: female sex, hypothyroidism, antidepressant use (can induce cycling), substance use. This patient has multiple risk factors. Antidepressant (sertraline) added 1 year ago correlates with accelerated cycling - strong evidence antidepressants can induce/worsen rapid cycling. Inadequately treated hypothyroidism (TSH 8.2) is also major contributor
cases.management: (1) STOP ANTIDEPRESSANT (sertraline) - strong evidence worsens rapid cycling; (2) Optimize thyroid treatment - increase levothyroxine to achieve TSH <2.5 (lower target than primary hypothyroidism); recheck in 6 weeks; (3) Review mood stabilizer: Consider LITHIUM (strongest evidence for rapid cycling) - target therapeutic 0.8-1.2; OR add valproate to lamotrigine; (4) Avoid antidepressants in future (controversial but many experts advise against in rapid cycling); (5) If no response: Consider combination mood stabilizers (lithium + valproate) or add atypical antipsychotic (quetiapine has evidence for bipolar depression); (6) Address alcohol use - worsens cycling; (7) Lifestyle: strict sleep-wake regularity, social rhythm therapy; (8) Intensive mood monitoring - daily mood charts; (9) Psychotherapy: IPSRT (Interpersonal and Social Rhythm Therapy); (10) Consider clozapine or ECT if refractory; (11) Long-term close monitoring - monthly initially; (12) Realistic expectations about course - may take 6-12 months to stabilize
